PNEUMOTHORAX
Definition: Pneumothorax is the presence of air or gas in the pleural cavity, leading to a collapsed lung. It can be spontaneous or traumatic.
Symptoms: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain and shortness of breath.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing a visible pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to the line. Upright imaging is preferred.
Treatment Guidelines: Small pneumothoraces may resolve spontaneously with oxygen therapy. Larger or symptomatic ones require needle aspiration or chest tube placement.

PNEUMONIA (COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED & HOSPITAL-ACQUIRED)
Definition: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs. The air sacs may fill with fluid or pus, causing cough with phlegm, fever, chills, and difficulty breathing.
Symptoms: Common symptoms include cough (often producing mucus), fever and sweating with shaking chills, shortness of breath, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and confusion.
Types: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the most common type. Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) develops 48+ hours after hospital admission. Aspiration pneumonia occurs from inhaling food, drink, or vomit.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray is the primary diagnostic tool showing infiltrates or consolidation. CT scan for complicated cases. Sputum culture and Gram stain. Blood cultures if bacteremia suspected. Procalcitonin levels to differentiate bacterial from viral.

PULMONARY EDEMA
Definition: Pulmonary edema is the accumulation of excess fluid in the lungs, usually due to heart failure (cardiogenic) but can be non-cardiogenic (e.g., ARDS).
Symptoms: Extreme shortness of breath, wheezing, feeling of suffocating, and frothy, blood-tinged sputum.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing bilateral symmetric opacities, Kerley B lines, cephalization of pulmonary vessels, and often cardiomegaly.
Treatment Guidelines: Diuretics (e.g., furosemide), vasodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin), and oxygen therapy. Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) may be necessary.

CARDIOMEGALY
Definition: Cardiomegaly is an enlarged heart, often a sign of an underlying condition such as heart failure, hypertension, or valvular heart disease.
Symptoms: Shortness of breath, dizziness, arrhythmias, edema (swelling) in the legs, and fatigue.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray reveals a cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) > 0.5. Echocardiogram is essential to determine the underlying cause and assess cardiac function.
Treatment Guidelines: Management targets the underlying cause. Medications may include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers. Lifestyle changes such as sodium restriction and weight management are recommended.

HEART FAILURE (AHA/ACC GUIDELINES)
Definition: Clinical syndrome where the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to meet metabolic demands of the body.
Symptoms: Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea (shortness of breath when lying flat), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower extremity edema, fatigue, sudden weight gain.
Diagnosis: Echocardiography to measure Ejection Fraction (HFrEF vs HFpEF). Elevated NT-proBNP or BNP. Chest X-ray showing cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5), pulmonary edema, Kerley B lines.
Treatment Guidelines: HFrEF quadruple therapy: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, Beta-blocker, MRA (spironolactone), SGLT2 inhibitor. Loop diuretics (furosemide) for volume overload symptom relief.

ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME (ACS)
Definition: Spectrum of conditions due to reduced blood flow to the heart muscle (unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI).
Symptoms: Chest pain (retrosternal pressure/heaviness), radiating to left arm or jaw, diaphoresis (sweating), nausea, shortness of breath.
Diagnosis: 12-lead ECG changes (ST elevation for STEMI, ST depression/T-wave inversion for NSTEMI), cardiac biomarkers (high-sensitivity Troponin I/T).
Treatment Guidelines: Initial emergency management: Oxygen if hypoxic, Sublingual Nitroglycerin, Aspirin (300mg chewable), Morphine for severe pain. Reperfusion therapy via Primary PCI within 90 minutes for STEMI. Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) + Anticoagulation.

STROKE (CEREBROVASCULAR ACCIDENT - ASA GUIDELINES)
Definition: Sudden focal neurological deficit caused by cerebrovascular cause (ischemic stroke 85%, hemorrhagic stroke 15%).
Symptoms: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty (FAST protocol), acute severe headache, loss of balance.
Diagnosis: Immediate Non-contrast Brain CT to rule out intracranial hemorrhage. Brain MRI for early ischemic changes.
Treatment Guidelines: Ischemic stroke: IV Thrombolysis (tPA/Alteplase) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Endovascular Thrombectomy (EVT) for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours. Hemorrhagic: BP management, neurosurgical intervention.

COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 RESPIRATORY INFECTION)
Definition: COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. It primarily affects the respiratory system but can impact multiple organ systems.
Symptoms: Common symptoms include fever or chills, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache, new loss of taste or smell, sore throat, congestion, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Diagnosis: RT-PCR (gold standard) from nasopharyngeal swab. Rapid antigen tests. Chest CT showing ground-glass opacities. Blood tests may show lymphopenia, elevated CRP, D-dimer, ferritin, and LDH.
Treatment Guidelines: Mild/moderate: Supportive care, antipyretics, adequate hydration. Moderate with risk factors: Antiviral therapy (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or remdesivir) within 5 days of symptom onset. Severe: Dexamethasone, remdesivir, tocilizumab or baricitinib for hyperinflammation. Critical: ICU care with mechanical ventilation.

PLEURAL EFFUSION
Definition: Pleural effusion is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space between the lungs and the chest wall.
Symptoms: Chest pain (pleuritic), dry nonproductive cough, dyspnea, and orthopnea.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray shows blunting of the costophrenic angle or a meniscus sign. Ultrasound or CT scan can detect smaller effusions. Thoracentesis is used for fluid analysis (transudate vs. exudate).
Treatment Guidelines: Treatment depends on the cause (e.g., diuretics for heart failure, antibiotics for infection). Therapeutic thoracentesis or chest tube drainage may be required for symptomatic relief.

CONSOLIDATION
Definition: Lung consolidation occurs when the air that usually fills the small airways in your lungs is replaced with something else, like fluid, pus, blood, or water.
Symptoms: Dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing a dense, homogeneous opacity with air bronchograms.
Treatment Guidelines: Treatment is directed at the underlying cause (e.g., antibiotics for pneumonia, diuretics for pulmonary edema).

HYPERTENSION (HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE)
Definition: Hypertension is a chronic medical condition in which blood pressure in the arteries is persistently elevated. Defined as SBP ≥130 mmHg or DBP ≥80 mmHg.
Symptoms: Most people with hypertension have no symptoms. Severe cases may include headaches, nosebleeds, dizziness, chest pain, shortness of breath, and visual changes.
Diagnosis: Blood pressure measured on at least 2-3 separate occasions. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) recommended. Stage 1: 130-139/80-89 mmHg. Stage 2: ≥140/≥90 mmHg. Hypertensive crisis: >180/>120 mmHg.
Treatment Guidelines: Lifestyle modifications (DASH diet, sodium restriction <2.3g/day, exercise 150 min/week). First-line medications: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, or thiazide diuretics. Target BP: <130/80 mmHg.

DIABETES MELLITUS (TYPE 1 & TYPE 2 - ADA GUIDELINES)
Definition: Metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.
Symptoms: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds.
Diagnostic Criteria: Fasting Plasma Glucose ≥126 mg/dL. 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL. HbA1c ≥6.5%. Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms.
Treatment Guidelines: Type 1: Basal-bolus insulin therapy. Type 2: Lifestyle management + Metformin first-line. Add SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs for high CV/CKD risk. Target HbA1c <7.0%.

Treatment Guidelines: Management targets the underlying cause. Medications may include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers. Lifestyle changes such as sodium restriction and weight management are recommended.

TUBERCULOSIS (PULMONARY & EXTRAPULMONARY)
Definition: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can affect other parts of the body.
Symptoms: Persistent cough lasting 3+ weeks, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), chest pain, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, chills, and loss of appetite.
Diagnosis: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux test). Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA). Chest X-ray showing upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or miliary pattern. Sputum smear microscopy for acid-fast bacilli. GeneXpert MTB/RIF for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection.
Treatment Guidelines: Standard regimen (drug-susceptible TB): Intensive phase (2 months): Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (HRZE). Continuation phase (4 months): Isoniazid + Rifampicin (HR). Total duration: 6 months minimum. Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is recommended.

PLEURAL THICKENING
Definition: Pleural thickening is a scarring or calcification of the pleura, often due to past inflammation, infection, asbestos exposure, or trauma.
Symptoms: Often asymptomatic. Extensive thickening can restrict lung expansion, causing dyspnea.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray or CT scan showing irregular thickening or calcified plaques along the chest wall.
Treatment Guidelines: Usually requires no specific treatment unless it causes severe restrictive lung disease.

ATELECTASIS
Definition: Atelectasis is the collapse or closure of a lung resulting in reduced or absent gas exchange. It may affect part or all of a lung and is typically caused by airway obstruction, lung compression, or loss of surfactant.
Symptoms: Small areas of atelectasis may be asymptomatic. Larger areas can cause dyspnea, rapid and shallow breathing, coughing, and low-grade fever.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing displacement of interlobar fissures, increased lung opacity, or elevation of the hemidiaphragm. CT scan for detailed assessment.
Treatment Guidelines: Deep breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and coughing. Bronchoscopy may be used to remove obstructions. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) or CPAP can help keep airways open.

EMPHYSEMA
Definition: Emphysema is a form of COPD characterized by the destruction of the alveoli, leading to enlarged air spaces and loss of lung elasticity.
Symptoms: Chronic, progressive dyspnea, especially with exertion, and a barrel chest.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing hyperinflated lungs, flattened diaphragm, and increased radiolucency. Spirometry confirms the diagnosis.
Treatment Guidelines: Smoking cessation, bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, pulmonary rehabilitation, and supplemental oxygen if hypoxic.

CONSOLIDATION
Definition: Lung consolidation occurs when the air that usually fills the small airways in your lungs is replaced with something else, like fluid, pus, blood, or water.
Symptoms: Dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing a dense, homogeneous opacity with air bronchograms.
Treatment Guidelines: Treatment is directed at the underlying cause (e.g., antibiotics for pneumonia, diuretics for pulmonary edema).

CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD - KDIGO GUIDELINES)
Definition: Abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for >3 months with implications for health.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic early; later fatigue, peripheral edema, pruritus, uremic symptoms.
Diagnosis: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² or persistent albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g).
Treatment Guidelines: SBP control <120 mmHg using ACEi or ARBs. SGLT2 inhibitors to slow CKD progression. Dialysis or kidney transplantation for Stage 5 ESRD.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION (UTI & PYELONEPHRITIS)
Definition: Bacterial infection of the urinary system (cystitis vs pyelonephritis).
Symptoms: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain. Pyelonephritis adds fever, chills, flank pain, CVA tenderness.
Diagnosis: Urinalysis (leukocyte esterase, nitrites), Urine Culture & Sensitivity.
Treatment Guidelines: Uncomplicated cystitis: Nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX or Fosfomycin. Pyelonephritis: Fluoroquinolones or IV Ceftriaxone.

PULMONARY MASS
Definition: A pulmonary mass is a localized lesion in the lung measuring greater than 3 cm in diameter. It is often suspicious for malignancy (lung cancer) but can be benign.
Symptoms: Often asymptomatic early on. Later symptoms may include chronic cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray identifies the mass. A contrast-enhanced CT scan, PET scan, and tissue biopsy (bronchoscopy or needle biopsy) are required to determine malignancy.
Treatment Guidelines: Management depends on the biopsy results. Malignant masses may require surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or targeted therapy.

ASTHMA (GINA GUIDELINES)
Definition: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterized by variable airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
Symptoms: Episodic wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough (often worse at night or early morning).
Triggers: Allergens, cold air, exercise, respiratory infections, smoke, stress.
Diagnosis: Spirometry showing reversible airflow obstruction (FEV1 increase ≥12% after bronchodilator). Peak expiratory flow variability.
Treatment Guidelines: Stepwise approach per GINA guidelines. SABA for relief. ICS (inhaled corticosteroids) as first-line controller. LABA + ICS for moderate/severe. Severe: biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab).

HIATAL / DIAPHRAGMATIC HERNIA
Definition: Protrusion of abdominal organs (like the stomach) into the chest cavity through the diaphragm.
Symptoms: Heartburn, chest pain, difficulty swallowing, or asymptomatic.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing a retrocardiac mass, sometimes with an air-fluid level.
Treatment Guidelines: Asymptomatic cases require no treatment. Symptomatic ones are treated with acid-suppressing medications (PPIs) or surgical repair if severe.

Definition: Clinical syndrome where the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to meet metabolic demands of the body.

Diagnosis: Echocardiography to measure Ejection Fraction (HFrEF vs HFpEF). Elevated NT-proBNP or BNP. Chest X-ray showing cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5), pulmonary edema, Kerley B lines.
Treatment Guidelines: HFrEF quadruple therapy: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, Beta-blocker, MRA (spironolactone), SGLT2 inhibitor. Loop diuretics (furosemide) for volume overload symptom relief.

Symptoms: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds.
Diagnostic Criteria: Fasting Plasma Glucose ≥126 mg/dL. 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL. HbA1c ≥6.5%. Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms.

TUBERCULOSIS (PULMONARY & EXTRAPULMONARY)
Definition: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) but can affect other parts of the body.
Symptoms: Persistent cough lasting 3+ weeks, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), chest pain, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, fever, night sweats, chills, and loss of appetite.
Diagnosis: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux test). Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA). Chest X-ray showing upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or miliary pattern. Sputum smear microscopy for acid-fast bacilli. GeneXpert MTB/RIF for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection.
Treatment Guidelines: Standard regimen (drug-susceptible TB): Intensive phase (2 months): Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (HRZE). Continuation phase (4 months): Isoniazid + Rifampicin (HR). Total duration: 6 months minimum. Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is recommended.

PNEUMONIA (COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED & HOSPITAL-ACQUIRED)
Definition: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs. The air sacs may fill with fluid or pus, causing cough with phlegm, fever, chills, and difficulty breathing.
Symptoms: Common symptoms include cough (often producing mucus), fever and sweating with shaking chills, shortness of breath, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and confusion.
Types: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the most common type. Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) develops 48+ hours after hospital admission. Aspiration pneumonia occurs from inhaling food, drink, or vomit.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray is the primary diagnostic tool showing infiltrates or consolidation. CT scan for complicated cases. Sputum culture and Gram stain. Blood cultures if bacteremia suspected. Procalcitonin levels to differentiate bacterial from viral.

COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 RESPIRATORY INFECTION)
Definition: COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. It primarily affects the respiratory system but can impact multiple organ systems.
Symptoms: Common symptoms include fever or chills, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache, new loss of taste or smell, sore throat, congestion, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Diagnosis: RT-PCR (gold standard) from nasopharyngeal swab. Rapid antigen tests. Chest CT showing ground-glass opacities. Blood tests may show lymphopenia, elevated CRP, D-dimer, ferritin, and LDH.
Treatment Guidelines: Mild/moderate: Supportive care, antipyretics, adequate hydration. Moderate with risk factors: Antiviral therapy (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or remdesivir) within 5 days of symptom onset. Severe: Dexamethasone, remdesivir, tocilizumab or baricitinib for hyperinflammation. Critical: ICU care with mechanical ventilation.

INFILTRATION
Definition: Pulmonary infiltration refers to the filling of lung air spaces with fluid, pus, blood, or cells, indicating an active pathological process such as infection or inflammation.
Symptoms: Cough, fever, dyspnea, and sputum production depending on the underlying etiology.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray shows ill-defined opacities without volume loss. Clinical correlation and further imaging or lab tests are needed to determine the specific cause.
Treatment Guidelines: Directed at the underlying cause. Bacterial infiltrates (pneumonia) require antibiotics; inflammatory causes may require corticosteroids.

PULMONARY EDEMA
Definition: Pulmonary edema is the accumulation of excess fluid in the lungs, usually due to heart failure (cardiogenic) but can be non-cardiogenic (e.g., ARDS).
Symptoms: Extreme shortness of breath, wheezing, feeling of suffocating, and frothy, blood-tinged sputum.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing bilateral symmetric opacities, Kerley B lines, cephalization of pulmonary vessels, and often cardiomegaly.
Treatment Guidelines: Diuretics (e.g., furosemide), vasodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin), and oxygen therapy. Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) may be necessary.

PNEUMOTHORAX
Definition: Pneumothorax is the presence of air or gas in the pleural cavity, leading to a collapsed lung. It can be spontaneous or traumatic.
Symptoms: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain and shortness of breath.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing a visible pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to the line. Upright imaging is preferred.
Treatment Guidelines: Small pneumothoraces may resolve spontaneously with oxygen therapy. Larger or symptomatic ones require needle aspiration or chest tube placement.

PLEURAL EFFUSION
Definition: Pleural effusion is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space between the lungs and the chest wall.
Symptoms: Chest pain (pleuritic), dry nonproductive cough, dyspnea, and orthopnea.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray shows blunting of the costophrenic angle or a meniscus sign. Ultrasound or CT scan can detect smaller effusions. Thoracentesis is used for fluid analysis (transudate vs. exudate).
Treatment Guidelines: Treatment depends on the cause (e.g., diuretics for heart failure, antibiotics for infection). Therapeutic thoracentesis or chest tube drainage may be required for symptomatic relief.

CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD - KDIGO GUIDELINES)
Definition: Abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for >3 months with implications for health.
Symptoms: Asymptomatic early; later fatigue, peripheral edema, pruritus, uremic symptoms.
Diagnosis: eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² or persistent albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g).
Treatment Guidelines: SBP control <120 mmHg using ACEi or ARBs. SGLT2 inhibitors to slow CKD progression. Dialysis or kidney transplantation for Stage 5 ESRD.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION (UTI & PYELONEPHRITIS)
Definition: Bacterial infection of the urinary system (cystitis vs pyelonephritis).
Symptoms: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain. Pyelonephritis adds fever, chills, flank pain, CVA tenderness.
Diagnosis: Urinalysis (leukocyte esterase, nitrites), Urine Culture & Sensitivity.
Treatment Guidelines: Uncomplicated cystitis: Nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX or Fosfomycin. Pyelonephritis: Fluoroquinolones or IV Ceftriaxone.

CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT & MULTIMODAL CONFLICT RESOLUTION PROTOCOL
Concordant Cases: Both Computer Vision (CXR) and Clinical Symptom Analysis align on diagnosis (e.g., CXR shows Consolidation + Patient has Fever/Cough -> High confidence Pneumonia).
Complementary Cases: CV model identifies imaging pathology while NLP identifies underlying etiology or risk factors (e.g., CXR shows Cardiomegaly + Patient reports Hypertension -> Complementary diagnosis).
Discordant Cases (Safety Warning): CV model predicts critical pathology (e.g., Pneumothorax or Pulmonary Edema) but patient symptoms do not report acute distress, OR vice versa.
Action for Discordant Cases: Trigger safety alert override, request urgent radiologist review, and flag potential asymptomatic or atypical presentation.

PULMONARY MASS
Definition: A pulmonary mass is a localized lesion in the lung measuring greater than 3 cm in diameter. It is often suspicious for malignancy (lung cancer) but can be benign.
Symptoms: Often asymptomatic early on. Later symptoms may include chronic cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray identifies the mass. A contrast-enhanced CT scan, PET scan, and tissue biopsy (bronchoscopy or needle biopsy) are required to determine malignancy.
Treatment Guidelines: Management depends on the biopsy results. Malignant masses may require surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or targeted therapy.

PULMONARY FIBROSIS
Definition: Pulmonary fibrosis is a condition where lung tissue becomes damaged and scarred, making it difficult for the lungs to function properly.
Symptoms: Progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, fatigue, and clubbing of fingers.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray showing reticular or reticulonodular opacities, primarily in the lower lung zones. High-resolution CT (HRCT) shows "honeycombing."
Treatment Guidelines: Antifibrotic medications (pirfenidone, nintedanib), oxygen therapy, and pulmonary rehabilitation. Lung transplantation may be considered in advanced cases.

HYPERTENSION (HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE)
Definition: Hypertension is a chronic medical condition in which blood pressure in the arteries is persistently elevated. Defined as SBP ≥130 mmHg or DBP ≥80 mmHg.
Symptoms: Most people with hypertension have no symptoms. Severe cases may include headaches, nosebleeds, dizziness, chest pain, shortness of breath, and visual changes.
Diagnosis: Blood pressure measured on at least 2-3 separate occasions. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) recommended. Stage 1: 130-139/80-89 mmHg. Stage 2: ≥140/≥90 mmHg. Hypertensive crisis: >180/>120 mmHg.
Treatment Guidelines: Lifestyle modifications (DASH diet, sodium restriction <2.3g/day, exercise 150 min/week). First-line medications: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, or thiazide diuretics. Target BP: <130/80 mmHg.

CARDIOMEGALY
Definition: Cardiomegaly is an enlarged heart, often a sign of an underlying condition such as heart failure, hypertension, or valvular heart disease.
Symptoms: Shortness of breath, dizziness, arrhythmias, edema (swelling) in the legs, and fatigue.
Diagnosis: Chest X-ray reveals a cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) > 0.5. Echocardiogram is essential to determine the underlying cause and assess cardiac function.
Treatment Guidelines: Management targets the underlying cause. Medications may include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers. Lifestyle changes such as sodium restriction and weight management are recommended.

ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME (ACS)
Definition: Spectrum of conditions due to reduced blood flow to the heart muscle (unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI).
Symptoms: Chest pain (retrosternal pressure/heaviness), radiating to left arm or jaw, diaphoresis (sweating), nausea, shortness of breath.
Diagnosis: 12-lead ECG changes (ST elevation for STEMI, ST depression/T-wave inversion for NSTEMI), cardiac biomarkers (high-sensitivity Troponin I/T).
Treatment Guidelines: Initial emergency management: Oxygen if hypoxic, Sublingual Nitroglycerin, Aspirin (300mg chewable), Morphine for severe pain. Reperfusion therapy via Primary PCI within 90 minutes for STEMI. Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) + Anticoagulation.
